subunit: Interacts with PHLPP. Interacts (active GTP-bound form preferentially) with RGS14. Interacts (when farnesylated) with PDE6D; this promotes dissociation from the cell membrane. Interacts with SOS1. Interacts (when farnesylated) with GPR31. Interacts with RAP1GDS1. Interacts (active GTP-bound form) with both SHOC2 and PP1c (all isoforms) to form a tertiary complex; SHOC2 and PP1c preferably bind M-Ras/MRAS, but they also bind K-Ras/KRAS, N-Ras/NRAS and H-Ras/HRAS. Interacts (GTP-bound form) with MAPKAP1/SIN1; inhibiting K-Ras/KRAS activity. Interacts (GDP-bound form) with LZTR1; this interaction mediates KRAS ubiquitination by BCR E3 ligase complex

complexes.name: KRAS-PIK3CA cellular-homeostasis regulatory complex
complexes.function: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) activation complex which acts as a molecular switch maintaining cellular homeostasis by coordinating a broad range of essential processes, including glucose absorption, anabolic metabolism, cell growth, and survival. Once active, PIK3CA phosphorylates its substrate, PIP2 (ChEBI:18348), to generate PIP3 (ChEBI:16618), which in turn activates downstream signalling, including the AKT-mTOR pathway. This promotes cell survival by inhibiting pro-apoptotic factors, stimulate cell growth and proliferation through mTORC1 activation, and regulates metabolism by enhancing glucose uptake and glycolysis. Mutations in KRAS and PIK3CA are implicated in various cancers. Notably, in endometrial carcinogenesis, KRAS and PIK3CA mutations are mutually exclusive and inversely correlated, suggesting that alterations in either gene may play equivalent roles in tumour development.
complexes.properties: In its basal state, PIK3CA exists as an autoinhibited heterodimer composed of a p85-alpha regulatory subunit and a p110-alpha catalytic subunit, in which p85-alpha suppresses the catalytic activity of p110-alpha. KRAS engages p110-alpha, recruiting PIK3CA to the plasma membrane and relieving its autoinhibition.

complexes.name: GTPase KRAS - Son of sevenless homolog 1 complex
complexes.function: A RAS GTPase complex responsible for intracellular transduction of signals received through cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases. KRAS and SOS1 allosterically activate each other: binding of inactive KRAS.GDP to SOS1 stimulates SOS1 nucleotide exchange activity which in turn leads to KRAS binding GTP in place of GDP. KRAS accounts for around 85% of RAS-related mutations which lead to several cancers (including pancreatic, colon and small intestine) and rasopathies and of these, the more abundant KRAS-4B isoform (P01116-2) is dominant.
complexes.properties: Controlled by SOS1, KRAS binds GTP via its G-domain allowing for cycling between its inactive physiological GDP-bound state to an active GTP-bound state. Binding to an allosteric RAS-GTP is thought to slow down SOS1 and RAS-GDP associating by at least 10-fold while accelerating nucleotide release by two orders of magnitude, suggesting that conformational changes in the SOS1-RAS-GDP ternary complex, leads to the rotation and opening of the helical hairpin. RAS's allosteric site functions as a positive feedback loop by activating SOS1's catalytic site upon RAS binding.

complexes.name: KRAS-RAF1, MAPK-cascade signal initiation complex
complexes.function: Serine/threonine kinase complex which regulates diverse cellular processes, including proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Active, membrane-bound KRAS binds and recruits RAF1 to the membrane, initiating the canonical KRAS-RAF1-MEK-ERK, MAPK signalling cascade. RAF1 activation (via dimerization) leads to sequential phosphorylation of MEK and then ERK. Activated ERK moves into the nucleus to regulate gene expression through phosphorylation of transcription factors. Mutations that maintain KRAS in its active, GTP-bound state drive constitutive MAPK pathway signalling and promote oncogenesis; KRAS represents the most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancers, accounting for approximately 80% of RAS-driven tumors.
complexes.properties: RAF1 has three conserved regions CR1-CR3: 1) CR1 contains the KRAS-binding domain (RBD) and cysteine-rich domain (CRD); 2) CR2 has a 14-3-3 recognition site; and 3) CR3 (C-terminal), contains the kinase domain and a second 14-3-3 binding site. In the inactive state, a 14-3-3 dimer binds phosphorylated serines in CR2 and CR3 to maintain autoinhibition. Membrane-bound active GTP-KRAS binds the RBD of RAF1, while KRAS's CRD interacts with phospholipids, relieving autoinhibition and enabling RAF activation. Dimerization of RAF1 through its N‐terminal RBD or RBD-CRD domains differentially alters the dimerization mode of KRAS on both anionic and neutral membranes, facilitating the stabilization of a heterotetrameric KRAS-RAF complexes formed via dimerization of preformed RAS-RAF heterodimers.

complexes.name: SHOC2-KRAS-PPP1CA complex
complexes.function: Holophosphatase complex which dephosphorylates members of RAF family proteins, RAF1 (P04049), BRAF (P15056) and ARAF (P10398) at key inhibitory phosphorylation sites Ser-259, Ser-365 and Ser-214, respectively, while eliminating inhibitory phosphorylation on RAF family proteins to potentiate MAPK signalling. Functions as a key regulator of RTK-RAS signalling, a pathway which regulates cell proliferation and survival through the MAP kinase cascade. Mutations mapped to protein-protein interfaces in the complex impair complex formation and stabilization. Gain-of-function and loss-of-function mutations in SHOC2 are linked to driving RASopathy and RAS-driven cancers including colorectal cancers.
complexes.properties: Tripartite molecular structure in which a crescent-shaped SHOC2 acts as a scaffolding component to bind PPP1CA and KRAS through its Leucine-rich repeat region, and SHOC2 further interacts with a cryptic RVxF binding pocket in the N-terminal disordered region of PPP1CA. Initial complex formation is mediated by SHOC2-PPP1CA interactions and is stabilized by binding of GTP-loaded KRAS. KRAS activation leads to membrane localization of the SKP complex and dephosphorylation of RAF family proteins. KRAS binds SHOC2 with lower affinity than MRAS (O14807), and while MRAS can outcompete KRAS interactions with SHOC2, the interaction sites and dephosphorylation sites on RAF family members are conserved.
